intro: Adapting models to new domains in time series breaks into three directions. First is aligning the model's reasoning across different time series, so it understands patterns in unfamiliar data. Second is learning which parts of the data are useful in any domain versus which are specific to one place. This matters because when you move to a new hospital or factory, you can reweight training toward good data or retrain selectively instead of from scratch, which saves time and labeled data. Third is generating synthetic time series that capture the domain's essential behavior without overfitting to specific conditions. These directions split because they target different levels: model reasoning, data quality and transfer, and data synthesis itself.

groups.label: Aligning and reasoning across time series
writeup: When a model answers questions about time series from different sources or domains, it must align its understanding. A patient's heart rate pattern in one hospital system might be recorded in beats per minute; another hospital might record it alongside oxygen levels and blood pressure. The model needs to ground its reasoning in the patterns themselves, not in surface details like units or sensor specifics.

PATRA tackles this by learning to recognize and align the actual patterns in time series, then reason over them in a balanced way. Instead of treating every value equally, it identifies which parts of the sequence matter for answering the question—a sudden spike in heart rate, a sustained elevation, a slow decline—and uses those aligned patterns to answer accurately. This matters because when you move a model to a new hospital or dataset, the raw numbers change but the clinical patterns should stay consistent. By grounding the model in patterns rather than raw values, PATRA generalize better across different time series sources without retraining.

groups.label: Assessing data quality and learning to transfer
writeup: When you have time series data from many sources—multiple hospitals, multiple factories, multiple weather stations—not all of it is equally useful for training. One hospital might have better sensors, cleaner records, or more complete patient histories, which means its data captures the true disease signal more faithfully. Another might have noisier data or missing values because its equipment or processes are less rigorous. If you train on low-quality data, your model learns to fit the noise and measurement artifacts, so the patterns it memorizes don't appear in cleaner domains. The challenge is sorting good data from bad without manually inspecting every sequence. If you had to hire an expert to label data quality, it would be slow and expensive. Doing it automatically means the model can learn what will transfer because it focuses on high-quality examples that reveal real patterns, not domain-specific quirks.

The LLM Judgment paper solves this by using a large language model to assign quality ratings to diverse time series, then meta-learning—learning how to learn—from those ratings. Instead of hand-labeling quality, the LLM identifies patterns like completeness (are there missing values?), consistency (do the values stay in a reasonable range?), and information density (does the sequence capture signal or mostly noise?). The model then learns to weight high-quality sequences more heavily during training, and to focus on features that appear in high-quality data across domains, because those features are more likely to be real patterns. They tested this on eleven different benchmarks across three kinds of tasks: classification, forecasting, and question-answering. On each one, quality-aware training improved how well models adapted to new domains, because models trained on curated data learned the underlying signal rather than domain quirks. The insight is straightforward: if you learn from high-quality examples, you pick up the real mechanisms, and those mechanisms work anywhere.

groups.label: Generating and matching time series across domains
writeup: Time series generation—creating synthetic sequences that look realistic—is useful for domain adaptation because synthetic data lets you augment scarce domains or study what a model learns from. But many generative models rely on pairwise similarity: they compare each point to every other point to decide what sequence to generate next. This is slow and can miss important global patterns that span the whole sequence, especially when you're trying to adapt to a new domain with different patterns.

Winformer improves generation by transcending pairwise matching and capturing patterns that span longer ranges. It recognizes recurring structures and dependencies across the whole sequence, not just local similarities. This lets it generate time series that are more realistic and more faithful to domain-specific dynamics. When evaluated on twelve real-world generation tasks, Winformer outperformed the previous best methods by an average of 10.67%. For domain adaptation, this matters because better generated sequences can serve as both training data for under-resourced domains and as test cases to measure whether your transfer learning actually works.
